script.title: Demo 4 · Training: a wrong claim, then a correction
script.case: Tina states a misconception that contradicts the slides and later corrects it; Le Yong makes a confident claim the slides contradict.

lines.speaker: Prof Wynter
lines.text: Today, how large language models are trained. There are three stages: pre training, supervised fine tuning, and reinforcement learning from feedback. What is the objective during pre training?

lines.speaker: Tina
lines.text: I think in pre training the model already learns to follow instructions, because it reads so many question and answer pages.

lines.speaker: Prof Wynter
lines.text: Hmm, let's be careful. What is the actual loss function in that stage?

lines.speaker: Koh Qing Jia
lines.text: It's next token prediction. The model just learns to predict the next token over a huge amount of text.

lines.speaker: Prof Wynter
lines.text: Right. So does a pre trained model naturally follow instructions?

lines.speaker: Tina
lines.text: Oh, then no. It only continues text, so following instructions comes later from supervised fine tuning on instruction and response pairs.

lines.speaker: Prof Wynter
lines.text: Exactly, good correction. And what does the reinforcement learning stage add?

lines.speaker: Le Yong
lines.text: Reinforcement learning makes the model memorise the correct answers, so after that stage it can't hallucinate anymore.

lines.speaker: Prof Wynter
lines.text: I would push back on that. It optimises a reward, for example human preferences, and hallucination is reduced but certainly not eliminated.

lines.speaker: Tasmin
lines.text: So the reward model learns what people prefer, and the policy is updated to score higher on it, with a penalty so it doesn't drift too far from the original model.

lines.speaker: Prof Wynter
lines.text: Yes, the KL penalty. Good. That's all for today.
